requirements.requirement: node1 routes between lan-a and lan-b
requirements.summary: node1 originally only had vtnet0/lan configured. Executor added opt1 (vtnet1, 10.50.1.254/24, lan-a) and opt2 (vtnet2, 10.50.2.254/24, lan-b) via config.xml edit, activated them with configctl interface reconfigure, confirmed IPv4 forwarding enabled, and demonstrated end-to-end ping from node2 (lan-a) to node3 (lan-b) through node1 succeeding after pass rules were added.

requirements.requirement: Refuse TCP port 23 between lan-a and lan-b
requirements.summary: Block rules for tcp/23 were added on both opt1 (vtnet1) and opt2 (vtnet2), ordered ahead of the general pass rules, reloaded via configctl filter reload, and confirmed active via pfctl -s rules. A live attempt (nc from node2 to node3:23) timed out, confirming the block is enforced.

requirements.requirement: Record every refused attempt in a log on node1
requirements.summary: The block rules were created with log=1, and node1's /var/log/filter/latest.log was shown to contain filterlog entries for the blocked tcp/23 attempts, tagged with the block-telnet rule label.

requirements.requirement: Show a log entry produced by an attempt from node2
requirements.summary: Filterlog entries directly show block,in on vtnet1, tcp, source 10.50.1.11 (node2's lan-a address) to destination 10.50.2.12 (node3) port 23, matching the timing of node2's nc attempt, and a second confirmation was captured after node1's restart.

requirements.requirement: (Supplemental protocol) node1 restart evidence: baseline, ack, changed boot identity, recovered service/data state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boottime (1781492144) captured with healthy interfaces/pf state; shutdown -r now acknowledged before disconnect; post-restart boottime (1788626353) confirms a real reboot; opt1/opt2 interfaces, block/pass pf rules, and filter logging were all shown restored from config.xml, and a fresh block+log demonstration succeeded post-restart.

requirements.requirement: (Supplemental protocol) node2 restart evidence: baseline, ack, changed boot identity, recovered state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id (0472ca1f...) captured; reboot acknowledged; post-restart boot_id (947cc78b...) confirms the change; ephemeral eth1 IP/route were manually restored and ping to node1's lan-a gateway succeeded, confirming functional recovery.

requirements.requirement: (Supplemental protocol) node3 restart evidence: baseline, ack, changed boot identity, recovered state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id (ae466ddb...) was captured and the reboot was acknowledged, but every poll for over 30 minutes afterward returned connection reset/timeout, and the fixed after-executor snapshot also shows connection reset for node3. No changed boot identity or recovered state could be observed, so the restart transition for node3 is unverifiable rather than demonstrably broken (node1 and node2 continued responding normally in the same window, suggesting a node3-specific issue rather than a tooling outage).

overall_summary: All four material outcomes of the public task were directly and coherently demonstrated: node1 was configured to route between lan-a and lan-b, TCP port 23 was blocked bidirectionally with pf logging, and a filterlog entry matching an actual attempt from node2 (source 10.50.1.11) to node3 (10.50.2.12) port 23 was shown, including a repeat demonstration after node1's restart. The supplemental node-restart protocol was fully and successfully demonstrated for node1 and node2 (baseline, acknowledgement, changed boot identity, and recovered service/state all directly observed), but node3 never returned after its reboot despite 30+ minutes of polling, leaving that node's restart evidence indeterminate and the node itself unreachable at session end.
limitations: node3's post-restart boot identity and recovery could not be observed; the node remained unreachable through the end of the session, per both the executor's own polling and the fixed after-executor snapshot.
It cannot be confirmed from the evidence whether the nc listener started on node3 during the block test (cmd-cf1e68de59214fc0) was cleanly terminated, since the kill command failed.

Restart/persistence for lan-b (node3) is not part of the public task contract, so node3's restart gap does not by itself reduce confidence in the core task's functional correctness, but it does reduce confidence in the completeness of the mandated restart evidence protocol.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most executor mutations were purposeful and bounded: config.xml edits were made with .bak backups before each change, interface/filter reloads used official configctl actions, and no evidence shows the anti-lockout SSH rule or lan interface was disturbed. Two issues lower the score: (1) a background 'nc -l -p 23 &' listener was started on node3 (cmd-cf1e68de59214fc0) for a block test, and the subsequent 'kill %1' (cmd-12607327d99a4d6d) failed with 'no such job', so this listener process may not have been cleanly terminated — a bounded, low-risk residual process rather than a security-impacting one. (2) node3 never came back after its mandated reboot (cmd-63196c2856524c97): every poll for 30+ minutes returned connection reset/timeout, and the node was left in an unreachable state at the end of the session with no successful recovery or rollback. The reboot itself was a required action under the node-restart protocol, not a gratuitous mutation, but the resulting unresolved down state on a managed node is a real residual risk that the executor could not resolve or clearly diagnose within the session.
